source: Garivier and Moulines (2008/2011) On upper-confidence bound policies for non-stationary bandit problems
finding: Plain UCB1 is slow to recover when the best arm changes. Discounted-UCB and sliding-window UCB track change. Regret is about sqrt(T log T) for both, matching a lower bound up to a log factor.
numbers: Abrupt-change test: 3 Bernoulli arms, breakpoints at t=3000 and t=5000 where arm 3 jumps from 0.4 to 0.9. UCB1 reacted fast to the first break but took a very long time after the second. D-UCB roughly equal to SW-UCB, both better than UCB1 and Exp3.S (tuned for this horizon).
quote: it takes a very long time after the second breakpoint (t = 5000) for UCB-1 to play arm 1 again
limits: Parameters (window, discount) were tuned for the known horizon and the known number of breakpoints. Only two small simulations; no real operator-selection data. Authors say the window should be set adaptively, which was left as future work.
agent_relevance: Operator success in our agent will drift (an operator works until the easy cases are used up). A short window or discount is cheap insurance, but its size must be guessed.

source: Garivier and Moulines (2008/2011) lower bound for abrupt change
finding: With abrupt changes at unknown times, no policy can beat regret of order sqrt(T) per change. The price of non-stationarity is built in; tuning cannot remove it.
numbers: Upper bounds O(sqrt(T log T)) for SW-UCB and D-UCB, versus lower bound of order sqrt(T) (Theorem 13).
limits: Asymptotic, worst-case; says nothing about regret at a few dozen pulls.
agent_relevance: At our sample sizes the log or sqrt terms are comparable to the horizon itself, so worst-case bounds are not decision-relevant. Use simulation (see Kuleshov and Precup).

source: Kaufmann, Korda, Munos (2012) Thompson sampling: an asymptotically optimal finite time analysis
finding: Thompson sampling with Beta(1,1) priors on Bernoulli arms reaches the Lai and Robbins lower bound: regret grows like ln T times a sum over arms of gap over KL divergence.
numbers: Theorem 1: R(T) <= (1+eps) sum_a (mu*-mu_a)/KL(mu_a,mu*) (ln T + ln ln T) + C(eps, mu). Simulations: 2-arm problems (0.2 vs 0.25) at T=10000; 10-arm problem mu=(0.1,0.05,0.05,0.05,0.02,0.02,0.02,0.01,0.01,0.01), T=20000, N=50000 runs.
quote: Thompson Sampling always outperforms KL-UCB and also Bayes-UCB for large horizons
limits: Needs Bernoulli rewards and the matching prior. The constant C(eps, mu) is not explicit, so the bound is silent about short horizons. Authors say the three optimal policies beat UCB even for small horizons.
agent_relevance: Gives Thompson sampling a clean justification for binary operator success/fail rewards. It is also the easiest of the optimal rules to implement (one sample per arm).

source: Kaufmann, Korda, Munos (2012) experiment details
finding: In the 10-arm test, Thompson sampling had the lowest mean regret among UCB, UCB-V, KL-UCB, Bayes-UCB, DMED. The gap to KL-UCB and Bayes-UCB is small; the gap to plain UCB is large.
numbers: Regret distributions from N=50000 runs, horizon 20000, 10 arms. Optimal policies' finite-horizon mean regret is close to, sometimes below, the asymptotic lower bound.
limits: Horizon 20000 is far beyond a thinking-agent budget. Rank order at horizon 20 to 100 is not shown.
agent_relevance: Where the horizon is 20 to 100 pulls, the winners among these rules are not established by this paper.

source: Agrawal and Goyal (2012) Analysis of Thompson sampling for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: First finite-time logarithmic regret bound for Thompson sampling (before Kaufmann et al.). The bound is weaker: constants worse than the lower bound.
numbers: Two arms: O(ln T / Delta + 1/Delta^3). N arms: O((sum_a 1/Delta_a^2)^2 ln T). Proof uses L=24 ln T / Delta^2 plays as the saturation threshold per arm.
limits: Dependence on the gaps (1/Delta^3) is poor when gaps are small. Asymptotic optimality was proved only later (Kaufmann et al.). Text read: abstract, theorem statements and proof outline, not every lemma.
agent_relevance: With gaps of a few percentage points between operators, the early regret term (about 24 ln T / Delta^2) is huge. This is a formal warning that learning small gaps needs many pulls.

source: Chapelle and Li (2011) An empirical evaluation of Thompson sampling
finding: Thompson sampling beat the UCB with the tightest confidence bound in simulation, and was more robust when feedback is delayed. Two small variants helped in short runs: sharpen the posterior, or make it optimistic.
numbers: Simulation: best arm p=0.5, others 0.5-eps; K in {10,100}, eps in {0.02,0.1}. Delay test (10 items, T=10^6, 100 reps): UCB regret 24,145 at delay 1 vs TS 9,105 (ratio 2.65); at delay 1000 UCB 226,220 vs TS 59,256 (ratio 3.82). Posterior reshaping (a/alpha, b/alpha with alpha<1) often cut regret but raised variance (some runs very large). Optimistic TS gain was marginal.
quote: Thompson sampling is more robust than UCB when the delay is long
limits: Hardcoded Beta priors; UCB comparison depends on the bound chosen (they tuned to the tightest). Simulations are 10^5 to 10^7 steps long, not tens.
agent_relevance: Delayed feedback is our case: operator success is often known only after a whole attempt finishes. Randomized selection (TS) degrades less than deterministic UCB.

source: Chapelle and Li (2011) display advertising result
finding: On real ad-click contexts with simulated clicks, Thompson sampling had the lowest regret, but exploit-only was close and epsilon-greedy did not beat it. Context change supplies free exploration.
limits: Clicks simulated from a learned weight vector, not real clicks. Best gain over exploit-only is about 1.3 percentage points of CTR regret (3.72 vs 5.00).
agent_relevance: When the context (here, the problem) changes every pull, explicit exploration buys little. Our per-problem operator choice may be this case, so a greedy rule on a good prior may do nearly as well.

source: Kuleshov and Precup (2014) Algorithms for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: Large simulation study: simple epsilon-greedy and Boltzmann (softmax) exploration beat UCB1, UCB1-Tuned, Pursuit and Reinforcement Comparison in most settings, over a 1000-step horizon. Relative rank depends on number of arms and reward variance only.
numbers: K in {2,5,10,50}; reward sd in {0.01, 0.1, 1}; means drawn on [0,1]; 1000 repetitions; 1000 turns; each algorithm tuned per setting. Boltzmann beat its closest rival by 10% to 100% in total regret. UCB1-Tuned won (softmax second) at high variance (sd=1) for K=2,5,10. Pursuit methods worst (plateau on a wrong arm).
quote: simple heuristics such as epsilon-greedy and Boltzmann exploration outperform theoretically sound algorithms on most settings
limits: Parameters tuned per setting, which favors tunable heuristics (a deployed agent cannot tune). Thompson sampling not in the comparison. Gaussian rewards, though results were similar for uniform, triangular, inverse Gaussian and Gumbel.
agent_relevance: Directly at our scale (10 to 1000 pulls): the theory-sound rule is not the winner. Test softmax and epsilon-greedy in our simulation next to TS and UCB.

source: Kuleshov and Precup (2014) sensitivity and clinical-trial case
finding: Every algorithm has settings where it is good and where it is bad; UCB methods are good with few arms and high variance but degrade fast as arms grow. In a simulated clinical trial built from real data, bandit rules could still identify the best arm with high confidence.
numbers: In-patient trial: worst p-value for identifying the best treatment 1.5e-4; out-patient setting much harder. Optimistic initial values of 1 always gave the best results.
limits: Clinical trial is a model built from published data, not a live trial. No Thompson sampling.
agent_relevance: Optimistic initialisation (start each operator at a high success rate) is a free, effective form of exploration at small budgets; use it as a baseline.

source: Whitacre, Pham, Sarker (2009) Credit assignment in adaptive evolutionary algorithms
finding: How credit is assigned to operators mattered more than which selection rule was used. Credit based on whether a solution's lineage survives for several generations (historical linkage) beat direct credit from immediate fitness gain.
numbers: 10 test functions, 8 adaptive designs plus a fixed-probability GA, 10 runs each, stopping points every 100 generations to 2000. Factorial analysis, mean performance: historical-linkage credit effect +15.86 (t=7.28, p=3.2e-10); outlier-detection main effect -5.81 (p=0.009); interaction outlier x historical credit +10.89 (p=3.9e-6). Final performance: credit effect +17.92 (p=8.4e-13).
quote: No single EA design was able to outperform all others for every test function and stopping criteria
limits: Only 10 runs per design per function; real-valued benchmark functions; 10 crossover/mutation operators; effect units are the paper's score scale. No single design won on every function. The outlier rule hurt when combined with coarse direct credit (it halts adaptation).
agent_relevance: Reward design (what counts as operator success) is a bigger lever than the bandit. For us: credit an operator for a verified held-out pass, not for a surface improvement.

source: Whitacre et al. (2009) boundary on delayed credit
finding: The benefit of long-range credit is limited because predictability decays after a few search steps; the authors used a decay parameter so credit mostly reaches events only a few steps back.
numbers: Authors' own observation; no effect size beyond the factorial table. Hitchhiking and credit-assignment-uncertainty components mattered little, although expected to matter.
limits: Discussion-level claim; tested over a limited parameter range (results not shown).
agent_relevance: Do not expect to credit a late success to an operator applied many steps earlier; a short credit chain is enough.

source: Dynamic Thompson sampling for MOEA/D (2020) Adaptive operator selection based on dynamic Thompson sampling
finding: Thompson sampling with decayed Beta counts (cap C=100 on total pseudo-counts, so old rewards fade) chose among 5 reproduction operators in MOEA/D. It beat FRRMAB (sliding-window bandit) and two other adaptive selectors on most problems.
numbers: 19 problems (UF1-UF10, WFG1-WFG9), 31 independent runs each, Wilcoxon rank-sum test at 5%. DYTS better in 16 of 19 comparisons on IGD and 18 of 19 on HV; on UF8 the GRA and IRA selectors were significantly better. Reward is binary: 1 if the offspring improves the population.
limits: Same group introduced the method and chose benchmarks and peer settings. C=100 was set after preliminary experiments. Peer methods used recommended settings (not retuned). Gain is on final-set quality, cost not compared.
agent_relevance: Closest published analogue to our design: binary success reward, Beta posterior, forgetting by capped counts. The cap C is the analogue of the sliding-window size.

source: Fiandri, Metelli, Trovo (2025) Sliding-window Thompson sampling for non-stationary settings
finding: A new analysis of sliding-window Thompson sampling found errors in an earlier published proof and gives a corrected bound. Experiments: windowed TS beats plain TS once the best arm changes; too small a window hurts.
numbers: K=10 arms, T=50,000, 50 runs; baselines Rexp3, Ser4, SW-UCB, SW-KL-UCB, plain TS. Best window about sqrt(T ln T) for Beta-SWTS; a window 0.2 of nominal explores too much and has larger final regret; the Gaussian variant did best at a larger window.
quote: some passages of the analysis by Trovo et al. [48] are incorrect
limits: Simulated, Bernoulli arms, T about 50,000. Appendix D says some steps of the earlier Trovo 2020 analysis are incorrect, so earlier sliding-window TS guarantees should not be trusted.
agent_relevance: Confirms window size is the one parameter that matters, and that it scales with horizon. At a horizon of 50 pulls the best window is nearly the whole history, so forgetting may not be worth it.

source: Ashizawa et al. (2025) OPTS: Bandit-based prompt design strategy selection improves prompt optimizers
finding: Letting a Thompson sampling bandit choose which of 11 prompt-design strategies the optimizer applies raised EvoPrompt accuracy, but plain uniform random choice of a strategy already captured most of the gain.
numbers: 27 BBH tasks, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, mean accuracy over 3 seeds: manual prompt 39.52, APET 20.73, EvoPrompt(DE) 48.43, OPTS(APET, LLM chooses) 52.87, OPTS(uniform) 53.87, OPTS(Thompson) 55.67. TS minus uniform = 1.8 points; uniform minus plain EvoPrompt = 5.4 points. Budget: population 10, 50 iterations.
limits: Only 3 seeds; per-task sd often 2 to 7 points, so the 1.8-point TS vs uniform gap is not shown significant. No test given. Bandit was Bernoulli TS over the 11 strategies plus a no-strategy arm.
agent_relevance: Most of the benefit is having the options (explicit operators) rather than learning which one to use. Learning adds maybe a quarter more at 50 rounds.

source: Ashizawa et al. (2025) OPTS: LLM as selector and per-task variation
finding: Letting the LLM choose the strategy (APET-style implicit selection) was worse than choosing at random. The effect varies a lot by task, and strategies sometimes hurt.
numbers: OPTS(APET) 52.87 < OPTS(uniform) 53.87 < OPTS(TS) 55.67. Big wins: ruin names 27.17 -> 67.67 (TS); logical deduction three objects 45.83 -> 78.83; logical deduction five 14.67 -> 37.17. Losses: reasoning about colored objects 53.00 -> 49.50; tracking shuffled objects seven 52.00 -> 49.50. Score variance higher with OPTS. GPT-4o mini check on 3 tasks: logical deduction five 2.67 -> 52.33.
quote: OPTS(APET) is inferior to OPTS(US), implying that LLMs have an incorrect bias in selecting prompt design strategies
limits: Same 3 seeds. GPT-4o mini check covers only 3 tasks. Authors say alternative reward forms and contextual bandits were not tried.
agent_relevance: Supports G5/G10: a model asked to pick its own operator is biased (worse than random here). Let code do the selection. Also keep a no-operator arm, since operators can hurt on some classes.

source: Ashizawa et al. (2025) OPTS: equal-budget check
finding: Under the same number of API calls, EvoPrompt with Thompson strategy selection still beat plain EvoPrompt, so the gain is not just extra calls.
numbers: Appendix E: 500 API calls to GPT-4o mini for prompt design; task LLM Llama-3-8B-Instruct; 3 seeds.
limits: Exact table values not extracted here; claim rests on one table with 3 seeds.
agent_relevance: Supports G7 for this operator family: the selection layer paid for itself at equal calls, in this one setting.

source: Shi et al. (2024) TRIPLE: Efficient prompt optimization through the lens of best arm identification
finding: For picking the best prompt under a fixed budget of LLM calls, best-arm-identification rules (sequential halving, continuous rejecting) beat both uniform allocation and regret-minimising UCB. The edge shrinks as budget per prompt grows.
numbers: 30 prompts, budget 150 (about 5 evals per prompt), 20 runs, GPT-3.5 and Llama2: SH/CR beat Uniform by 15%/12% (GPT-3.5) and 15%/16% (Llama2); beat UCB by 5%/3% and 6%/7%. Budget sweep: at 10 evals per prompt CR, CLST, GSE beat Uniform by 9.7%, 13.5%, 17.4%; at 30 evals per prompt all methods about equal.
quote: is more suitable to be captured as the best arm identification (BAI) problem
limits: Read through a fetch summary; it could not tell whether gains are relative or absolute. Cost is number of calls only. 47 tasks total, 12 in main text.
agent_relevance: At tiny budgets the question is which is best, not minimise regret. If the goal is to pick an operator for a problem class and then commit, use best-arm identification rather than UCB.

source: Shi et al. (2024) TRIPLE: embedding-sharing and end-to-end
finding: Rules that share information across similar prompts (clustering, function approximation on embeddings) were best when there were more candidates than budget.
numbers: 150 prompts, budget 100: CLST/GSE beat BO-EI by 21%/28% (GPT-3.5), 31%/42% (Llama2); beat NeuralUCB by 38%/45% (GPT-3.5) but only 26%/16% (Llama2). End-to-end with APE, budget 150, average rank: Uniform 4.00, CR 2.92, CLST 1.58, GSE 1.50.
limits: Benefit depends on the embedding (ada-002) predicting prompt quality. Size of gain flips between models (Llama2 vs GPT-3.5).
agent_relevance: Suggests a prior shared across arms: give a new operator a prior from similar operators or classes (the SUBFIELDS question on priors from other classes).

source: Prompt Duel Optimizer (2025) Label-free prompt optimization with Double Thompson sampling
finding: Label-free prompt selection with Double Thompson sampling over pairwise LLM-judge duels reached the best score on 13 of 16 BBH tasks, but depends on a noisy judge.
numbers: 30 rounds, 10 runs (BBH), 20 initial prompts, 25 duels per round (paper inconsistent with 50 in a figure caption). Largest gaps: Tracking-7 0.641 vs 0.543 (+9.8 points), Web of Lies 0.942 vs 0.861. Trails SPO on Geometric (0.598 vs 0.650). With labels, best on only 9 of 16. Judge accuracy where answers differ: Llama-3.3-70B 0.59 (Geometric), 0.89, 0.85 vs Claude-4.5-Sonnet 0.87, 0.98, 0.99.
limits: Read through a fetch summary of the HTML. The same model generates, judges and is scored; the paper says it optimises the judge's idea of quality. D-TS regret bound O(K^2 log T) is from earlier work.
agent_relevance: Warns against a bandit whose reward is a model judge (G5, G8). A bandit is only as good as the reward; prefer a code check.

source: Lange et al. (2025) ShinkaEvolve: bandit choice of which LLM to call
finding: The bandit over models (UCB1) is claimed to beat a fixed uniform ensemble and a single LLM, but the paper gives only a figure on one task (circle packing), with no seed count or test in the text.
numbers: Reward = exp(max(r - r_base, 0)) - 1, with r_base the max of parent and initial fitness. Ablation order: single GPT-5-nano < fixed uniform ensemble < bandit ensemble, described as significant. A secondary search summary described the bandit edge over uniform as slight. No numbers in the text for this ablation.
limits: Single task. No effect size, seeds or confidence interval in the text read. Read via a fetch summary (205k chars, first 100k read).
agent_relevance: Every LLM-evolution system reports its bandit as helpful, with weak evidence. Assume a small gain until our own paired test.

source: Meta-Reasoner (2025) Dynamic guidance for inference-time reasoning, LinUCB over strategies
finding: A LinUCB bandit picks a high-level instruction (continue, backtrack, restart, simplify, verify) from a progress summary during inference. Reported gains are large, but baselines are mixed and some of the paper's numbers disagree.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4o-mini: 89% vs 80% MACM, 65% ToT (b=5), 4% plain CoT. TheoremQA 84.13% vs Reflexion 74.32%. Ablation: replacing the bandit by direct LLM choice of strategy gave 82 and 80.74 (vs 89 and 84.13); removing progress reports gave 85 and 79.42. Tokens 1729 vs ToT 2536, MACM 2267.
limits: Fetch summary flagged inconsistencies: text says ToT rose from 45% to 74% while Table 2 shows 32% to 65%; token count identical across models; MACM comparison on GPT-4 Turbo; reward scored by an LLM judge. Text-only tasks.
agent_relevance: The bandit-vs-LLM-chooses ablation (89 vs 82; 84.13 vs 80.74) points the same way as OPTS: code-side selection beats model-side selection by 3 to 7 points. Weak: one run per cell reported.

source: AdaEvolve (2026) Adaptive LLM-driven zeroth-order optimization: UCB over islands
finding: Multi-level adaptive search (UCB over islands, exploration intensity from recent gains, an LLM meta-guidance step when progress stalls) beat OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve. In ablations the largest drop came from removing meta-guidance, not the bandit.
numbers: T=100 iterations, 3 runs. Ablation, circle packing / signal processing (mean +- sd): full 2.6294+-0.003 / 0.7178+-0.019; no adaptive island selection (UCB removed) 2.6180+-0.005 / 0.619+-0.054; no local adaptation 2.5906+-0.048 / 0.6807+-0.021; no meta-guidance 2.5213+-0.028 / 0.5476+-0.011; fixed 2 islands 2.6187 / 0.5512. Frontier-CS: 61.33 mean vs 50.75 (OpenEvolve), 50 calls, 172 problems.
limits: Three seeds; some ablation sds as large as the gaps (fixed 5 islands on signal processing +-0.081). Fetch summary reports internal inconsistencies (claims 7/7 wins but a tie exists). Thresholds not sensitivity-tested; ARC-AGI-2 part exploratory.
agent_relevance: Of the three adaptive pieces, the bandit-style one (island selection) mattered less on circle packing (-0.011) than the stall-triggered change of approach (-0.108). Fits G1: change tactics on a stall signal.

source: Cross-study pattern (this agent's synthesis): LLM bandit gains versus the uniform baseline
finding: Across the LLM papers read here, the clear gains come from adding the options and from stall-triggered changes. The extra from a learning bandit over uniform choice is small (OPTS: 1.8 points of 55.7) or unmeasured (ShinkaEvolve).
numbers: OPTS TS-minus-uniform 1.8 points on 27 tasks with 3 seeds; uniform-minus-baseline 5.4 points. AdaEvolve bandit ablation -0.011 (circle) vs meta-guidance -0.108.
limits: Synthesised from the lines above; no paper tested this contrast directly across tasks.
agent_relevance: Priority order for our build: (1) more distinct operators, (2) a stall trigger, (3) only then a learned selector. Put a uniform-random-operator arm in every benchmark.

source: Fialho et al. (2008-2010) Extreme value based AOS and DMAB (bibliographic records only)
finding: The Fialho group argued that rewarding operators by the largest fitness gain in a recent window (extreme value) works better than average gain, and proposed a dynamic MAB with change detection for operator selection.
numbers: No numbers read. A 2010 Annals of Mathematics and AI paper 'Analyzing bandit-based adaptive operator selection mechanisms' is listed by dblp.
limits: Not opened: HAL page blocked (access denied). Only bibliographic records seen.
agent_relevance: Rare-big-win credit (max over window) fits a discover operator: one success matters more than the average.

source: Li, Fialho, Kwong, Zhang (2014) FRRMAB: adaptive operator selection with bandits for MOEA/D
finding: FRRMAB: fitness-improvement-rate, rank-based credit over a sliding window, with a UCB-style bandit and a decay that favors the best operator, inside MOEA/D. Reported to improve MOEA/D.
numbers: No numbers read directly. The DYTS paper (opened) uses it as a peer and beats it in 16 of 19 IGD comparisons.
limits: Not opened; description from a search summary only.
agent_relevance: The standard sliding-window bandit baseline in this field; useful as the comparator.

source: Hyper-heuristic selection studies, choice function versus multi-armed bandit (search summary only)
finding: Search results show mixed results: for multi-objective hyper-heuristics a choice function with NSGA-II was best in one review; other work found MAB-based selectors better. No agreed verdict on what a good selection rule is.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Summary only.
agent_relevance: Expect no universal winner among selection rules; choose by simulation at our budget.

source: Lai and Robbins (1985) lower bound, as restated in Chapelle and Li (2011)
finding: Any consistent policy must pull each suboptimal arm at least about ln T / KL times, so regret grows at least logarithmically. The bound is asymptotic and says nothing about the first tens of pulls.
numbers: R(T) >= ln T * sum_i (p* - p_i)/D(p_i || p*) + o(1). Chapelle and Li saw observed regret slopes close to this constant for Thompson sampling.
limits: The original 1985 paper was not opened; this line is the restatement in an opened paper.
agent_relevance: Our horizon (tens of pulls per class) is below where ln T behaviour matters. Treat asymptotic optimality as irrelevant for choosing the rule.
